content: The provision of the dapivirine vaginal ring to women should be integrated with other prevention strategies and health services. This includes the availability of condoms, a variety of contraceptive methods, testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and access to or referrals for services aimed at preventing and addressing gender-based violence. Where feasible, voluntary partner services should also be considered. HIV testing is recommended prior to initiating the use of the dapivirine vaginal ring and should be repeated every three months during its use as part of the service package. Although studies have not directly compared oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with the dapivirine vaginal ring, current evidence suggests that daily oral PrEP, when taken as prescribed, is more effective in preventing HIV than the vaginal ring. Oral PrEP should be offered at sites where the dapivirine vaginal ring is provided, allowing women to make an informed choice. Women should receive comprehensive information and counseling on the available prevention options, including their relative efficacy and safety, to help them make the best decision for their needs. The dapivirine vaginal ring has not demonstrated efficacy among women younger than 21 years, primarily due to low adherence in this age group. Additional data are needed to understand its use among younger women. Experience with oral PrEP services for adolescent girls and young women indicates that younger women may require additional support, particularly during the early stages of use, to ensure continuation. This may also apply to the dapivirine vaginal ring, and ongoing or planned studies aim to address implementation challenges, adherence issues, and effectiveness in this demographic. There is no current experience with providing the dapivirine vaginal ring to key populations, such as sex workers and women who use drugs. However, it is expected to offer protection against HIV transmission via vaginal sex for these groups. Before targeted implementation, it is essential to understand and consider the values and preferences of women from key populations to determine whether they find the ring acceptable and beneficial. Community engagement will be critical in designing and delivering programs tailored to their needs. The dapivirine vaginal ring has not yet been provided outside of research and open-label extension projects. Careful consideration, including engagement with women and healthcare providers, is necessary to determine the most appropriate delivery sites. These could include reproductive health services, STI services, contraception services, gender-based violence services, youth-friendly services, and other settings where oral PrEP is available. Special considerations will be required to ensure safe and acceptable approaches for women from key populations. Demonstration projects can help identify the best sites for offering the ring. Like oral daily PrEP, the dapivirine vaginal ring must be used consistently as prescribed to be effective. Adherence support should be a central component of service provision, with flexible and tailored support provided, especially during the initial stages of use. Frequent check-ins with healthcare or lay providers may be necessary to support adherence. Additional support should be considered for younger women, and partner and peer support may also be beneficial. The dapivirine vaginal ring is a new product, and in many communities where women face a high risk of HIV, there may be little or no awareness of vaginal ring products. Awareness programs for both the community and providers should be developed and implemented before and during the introduction of the ring. These programs should engage women’s networks and address concerns and questions about the product. Messaging for men and male partners should also be considered, as some women have reported that discussing ring use with their partners was supportive and helpful for continued use. The dapivirine vaginal ring is a new product, and provider experience with vaginal ring products is likely limited in settings with a high burden of HIV. National programs should ensure adequate training and ongoing mentoring for providers to support the development and delivery of this service. Understanding and addressing provider concerns will be essential. Monthly use of the dapivirine vaginal ring has been shown to be safe and effective for HIV prevention among non-pregnant women of reproductive age. However, data on its effects during pregnancy and breastfeeding are limited. Animal toxicity studies have not identified adverse effects on maternal health or fetal development. In the ASPIRE trial, no adverse effects on pregnancy or infant outcomes were observed among women who became pregnant during the trial. However, further safety studies are needed to evaluate its use during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Ongoing studies, such as MTN-042 (DELIVER) and MTN-043 (B-PROTECTED), aim to provide additional safety data. If no safety concerns are identified, post-market surveillance will be necessary to monitor pregnancy and fetal outcomes. A subanalysis of women younger than 21 years did not demonstrate efficacy in this age group, and adherence to the product was low. Further studies, such as MTN-034 (REACH), are underway to assess feasibility, effectiveness, and barriers to use in this demographic, as well as strategies to support adherence and continuation. There has been no research to date on implementing the dapivirine vaginal ring with key population groups, such as sex workers and women who use drugs. Conducting surveys to understand the values and preferences of these communities will be important. If the communities find the ring to be an important additional HIV prevention option, involving them in program design and development will be critical. Women will be counseled on the dapivirine vaginal ring alongside other prevention options, such as daily oral PrEP. Male and female condoms and partner services must also be available and offered alongside the ring. Some women may switch between oral PrEP and the vaginal ring or use both simultaneously. While using both products together is likely safe, there is no evidence of additive benefits. Adherence is crucial to optimize protection, and inconsistent use of either or both products would be ineffective for HIV prevention. Further research is needed to understand the use of the ring in combination with other prevention interventions and the patterns of switching between products. The dapivirine vaginal ring and oral daily PrEP are costly prevention interventions. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends prioritizing these options for women at substantial risk of HIV, as their use could provide the greatest benefit and be most cost-effective. Further cost-effectiveness analyses using real-world data in various settings and populations would be valuable to guide future implementation for maximum impact.
